purpose: Pertuzumab is used to treat a type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer. It is often given along with another medicine called trastuzumab (Herceptin) and chemotherapy. It can be used before surgery to shrink the tumor, after surgery to lower the chance of cancer coming back, or for breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body.
how_it_works: Some breast cancer cells have too many copies of a protein called HER2 on their surface, which helps the cancer grow quickly. Pertuzumab is a special antibody — like a guided missile — that attaches to the HER2 protein and blocks signals that tell the cancer cell to grow and multiply. By blocking these signals, it helps slow down or stop the cancer from spreading.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea (very common), nausea and vomiting, feeling very tired, hair loss, rash or skin problems, mouth sores, low blood cell counts (which can increase your risk of infections or bleeding), and numbness or tingling in your hands and feet.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious heart problems, including a weakened heart muscle, so your doctor will check your heart regularly with tests like an echocardiogram before and during treatment. It must NOT be used during pregnancy because it can seriously harm or cause the death of an unborn baby — use reliable birth control during treatment and for 7 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you have shortness of breath, swelling in your legs, or a fast or irregular heartbeat. Serious allergic or infusion reactions can also happen during or after the IV infusion.
typical_dosing: Pertuzumab is given through an IV (into a vein) by a healthcare professional, usually once every 3 weeks. The first dose is typically 840 mg, and then each dose after that is 420 mg. The infusion usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. Your doctor will decide exactly how long you need to receive this treatment based on your situation.
